title: The right, and what prior approval is not
paras: Class MA — and first, what prior approval is not. It changes the use of a building, and any curtilage land, from Class E — commercial, business and service — to residential: the main route by which commercial premises like shops, offices, gyms, clinics and light industrial become housing without a planning application. It's been with us since 2021, replacing office-to-residential and sweeping up the piecemeal commercial rights once those uses folded into Class E in 2020. The references and dates are in the written guide.

The permission comes from the order itself — these rights are grants of planning permission — so what you get isn't permission, it's prior approval of a closed list of matters. The change of use is settled, so the authority can't refuse because residential is unacceptable in principle, or the employment floorspace should be kept, or the scheme conflicts with the development plan. The plan is largely out: there's regard to national policy, but only so far as it bears on the listed matters. A policy simply hostile to conversion can't found a refusal — the only route to that is an Article 4 direction.

So no affordable housing through prior approval, and conditions can't reach beyond the listed matters, though the Community Infrastructure Levy can still be payable — the in-use buildings deduction often reduces or wipes it out. The mechanics: a fifty-six day period, deemed consent if the authority stays silent, and a fee per dwelling, currently two hundred and sixty pounds, well below the application fee; fees change, so check. And it's no formality — applications fail regularly, most often on natural light, noise and transport, and a scheme that doesn't comply with every limitation and condition gains nothing.

title: Qualifying buildings: the gateway tests
paras: Which buildings qualify. The gateway: Class E use for a continuous two years, ending on the application date — the period runs to the application, not the change of use. For any part before the September 2020 reforms, the use must have sat within the old predecessor classes — shop, office, light industrial, certain community and leisure — so something in Class E today but outside those then can still fail. And it must be lawful; a breach can't count unless time has made it lawful, in which case take a certificate of lawfulness first.

The 2024 changes dropped the three-month vacancy requirement and the fifteen hundred square metre floorspace cap, so occupied buildings of any size, big office blocks included, now go through. But vacancy still matters: a vacant building keeps its last lawful use and short periods won't break continuity, but a long-vacant one raises whether the Class E use subsisted or had been abandoned — fact and degree. Older commentary on the vacancy rule or the cap is the 2021-to-2024 law, history now.

The exclusions are absolute — no discretion. Not permitted where the land is, or forms part of, a site of special scientific interest, a listed building or land in its curtilage, a scheduled monument or its curtilage, a safety hazard area or a military explosives storage area — nor a National Landscape, still called an area of outstanding natural beauty, a National Park, the Broads, a World Heritage Site, or a few other designated areas. The listed exclusion reaches unlisted buildings in a listed building's curtilage. But conservation areas are deliberately left off — MA applies there, subject to an extra ground-floor matter, which a lot of people get wrong. And an agricultural tenancy needs the documented consent of both landlord and tenant.

The development is the change of use of the building and any curtilage land — partial conversion works, ground-floor commercial with flats above, the tests applied to the building and the matters to what's proposed. The end use must be C3 and nothing else, so houses in multiple occupation, serviced apartments and short-term letting all fall outside, and it must stay residential afterwards. And the sui generis uses — the takeaway, betting office, pub, launderette — were never Class E, so they can't use MA at all, though some keep rights under other Classes.

title: The 56 days, deemed consent and implementation
paras: Procedure. You apply for a determination whether prior approval is required for the matters — three outcomes: not required; required and given; or required and refused, and refusal on any one defeats the whole. The content is a description, plan, contact details and fee, but in practice you need floor plans showing the number of dwellings, the layout and window positions and dimensions, because you can't judge natural light without them. The authority can refuse where the scheme doesn't comply, or where it hasn't enough to judge — and that refusal carries a right of appeal, the proper route where it thinks the scheme is outside MA altogether. Consultation goes to the highway authority, the Environment Agency where there's flooding, and the neighbours.

You can't begin before written notice, or fifty-six days from receipt — whichever comes first. That's the deemed consent. Three qualifications matter. The clock runs from receipt of a valid application, and disputes about when it started, over fees or electronic submission, are common. It can be extended only by written agreement — an exchange of emails will do, read objectively. And deemed consent adds nothing if the development doesn't qualify: silence can't turn non-qualifying development into permitted development, so proceeding after fifty-six days with gateway doubts is the developer's risk.

The determination is confined to the listed matters, with regard to representations and national policy so far as relevant. Conditions can only go on where reasonably related to the subject matter, so a general development-management condition is unlawful. A refusal — or a non-determination where an extension removed the deemed consent — carries the usual right of appeal, normally by written representations, on the same matters. And when certainty really matters, funders, purchasers, a marginal case, only a lawful development certificate gives a conclusive presumption of lawfulness; neither prior approval nor deemed consent does.

Two conditions ride on the development, both biting harder than their planning-permission cousins. It must be completed — not just commenced — within three years of the approval date, the date approval is given or the fifty-sixth day where nothing was notified; a stalled conversion that misses it loses the right. And it must be carried out to the approved details, or on deemed consent the application details. There's no amendment mechanism for a prior approval — none of the usual routes to vary a permission apply — so a design change after approval needs a fresh prior approval, or a planning application for the changed element, secured before it's built.

title: The prior approval matters — and what is not one
paras: The matters are exhaustive, each judged alone. Transport is the impacts — safe vehicular and pedestrian access, servicing, refuse, intensification; parking stress counts where it bears on safety or the network, but local plan parking standards can't be applied as if this were an application, and the trip comparison against the lawful commercial use often shows a net reduction. Contamination is the safety of occupiers — a phase one desk study at minimum, more where the site has an industrial history. Flooding is the risk to the building — the Environment Agency consulted, a site-specific flood risk assessment in the higher-risk zones; the sequential test doesn't govern, but the substance of national flood policy comes in through the have-regard duty, and ground-floor residential in high-risk zones is the battleground.

Noise from commercial premises on the occupiers is one of the two most common refusals — agent-of-change in reverse, protecting incoming residents and, through them, the existing businesses from complaints. It's noise from commercial premises, not traffic generally. Expect a qualified acoustician, survey data over representative operating periods including night time where neighbours trade late, and mitigation through glazing and ventilation not reliant on sealed windows unless alternative ventilation is adequate. In a conservation area, ground-floor changes pick up an extra matter — the impact of losing the ground-floor use on the character or sustainability of the area, the counterweight to conservation areas not being excluded. Its scope is the change of use, not external appearance, answered with vacancy history, marketing evidence and the surrounding pattern of uses.

Natural light in every habitable room is the single most common refusal, brought in in 2020 after criticism of poor office conversions. Every habitable room — including kitchens used as living space, and bedrooms — must get adequate light, and 'adequate' is undefined, so it's planning judgment, usually daylight modelling against recognised guidance; lightwell-only, deep single-aspect and north-facing rooms get the closest scrutiny, and without floor plans showing window positions and dimensions the authority can refuse. The industrial areas matter protects occupiers' living conditions where housing goes into an area important for industry, waste or distribution; it is not a power to protect employment land, and refusing to protect employment stock under it errs in law. And the one loss-of-use matter is confined to registered nurseries and NHS health centres, answered with alternative provision, spare capacity, or cessation regardless.

What the authority can't consider decides as many appeals as what it can. Not matters: losing commercial or employment floorspace outside those two categories; internal space beyond the minimum floor area; amenity space, refuse or play space; design and external appearance absent operational works; affordable housing; and conformity with the development plan. Representations on those are received and considered, but can't found a refusal.

title: The case law: what prior approval cannot do
paras: The case law. The foundation is Keenan: prior approval can't enlarge the Class. A council's failure to respond in time didn't give permission to something that never qualified — neither a positive determination nor expiry of the period confers permission on development outside the Class. For MA that's fundamental: deemed consent is worthless if the building fails the two-year test, sits in an excluded designation, or otherwise breaches the gateway, and a granted approval can't cure it either. An authority's error in approving a non-qualifying scheme creates no permission, and a completed conversion on a defective claim is enforceable. The converse, from Murrell: where it does qualify, permission crystallises at expiry and the authority can't resile.

New World Payphones applies that to composition: the whole of a development must fall within the Class — description, exceptions, limitations, conditions. A mixed or dual-purpose scheme with one component outside isn't permitted development, and you can't sever the compliant core from the non-compliant whole afterwards. For MA that bites where the change of use is bundled with something the Class doesn't permit — operational development, uses outside C3, land beyond the curtilage — so structure it correctly, with separate applications for what MA doesn't cover.

Dharmeshkumar is the clearest modern statement that prior approval isn't a licence for the general concept of conversion. An office block converted to flats departed from the application drawings, and the redevelopment works were unlawful. The change of use lost the benefit on two independent grounds: unlawful operations associated with it strip it of the order's protection; and the condition tying it to the approved details, with the drawings read across where the notice is ambiguous. So build what was approved, keep the works lawful, and where the scheme changes get a fresh approval or a planning application for the changed element before you build — there's no amendment route.

Around those sits settled orthodoxy, worth re-checking before you cite it. The scope of a matter is statutory construction, for the courts; applying it to the facts is planning judgment, reviewable only on public law grounds. The matters are read purposively, not narrowly. Refusal on grounds outside the list is unlawful. Adequacy of light is judgment on the evidence, refusal proper where it isn't shown for every habitable room. Continuity of use, abandonment during vacancy and the extent of curtilage are all fact and degree. And separately, the permission is disapplied for any dwelling under thirty-seven square metres gross internal area, or failing the nationally described space standard — schemes have failed on unit sizes even where light and noise were sound.

title: Article 4, appraisal order and transactions
paras: Finally, Article 4, the appraisal order, and transactions. An Article 4 direction takes MA out of a defined area and restores full development-management control, the development plan included; it doesn't prohibit conversion or presume against it — it requires an application. And because the industrial-areas matter protects occupiers not employment land, and loss-of-use is confined to nurseries and health centres, an Article 4 direction is the only lawful way to protect commercial floorspace from MA — which is why they're widespread in London and strong office markets.

Two things discipline it. National policy says such directions should be limited to where necessary to avoid wholly unacceptable adverse impacts, on robust evidence, over the smallest area possible — and the Secretary of State can modify or cancel them, and has, against over-extensive ones. The other is compensation: withdraw the right, refuse what it would have permitted, and compensation for abortive expenditure and depreciation can follow unless sufficient notice was given. That's why most MA directions are non-immediate, with at least twelve months' notice — which is also the developer's window. A valid application made before the direction takes effect is determined under the right as it stood, and an approval already secured isn't removed by a later direction, though delaying with one pending is unwise.

The appraisal order. Start with Article 4 directions, confirmed and proposed — the mapped boundary and what's withdrawn. Then the absolute exclusions, curtilage listing included. Then two years of lawful Class E use, with the September 2020 lookback. Then space standards against the proposed layout. Then the matters in order of risk — natural light first, noise second. The failures mirror that order: daylight absent or inadequate; qualifying-use misunderstandings; vacancy-and-abandonment confusion; units below the space standard; curtilage-listed structures missed; noise surveys that missed operating hours; vagueness about which parts change use; and implementation failures — off-drawing builds, unlawful works, the missed completion deadline.

On transactions, due diligence must establish four things, with evidence: that the building qualified at the application date; that it was built to the approved details; that completion fell inside the three-year window; and that any external works had their own permission. Where any is doubtful, the lawful development certificate is the remedy — the prior approval documents alone prove none. And on an acquisition for conversion, check proposed directions as well as confirmed ones, and price that twelve-month notice window into the programme.
